title: Shop relayout sequenced to avoid a shutdown
tagline: 5S layout planning in SketchUp for a working custom-tooling shop
summary: I modeled Ely Tool's main floor to scale in SketchUp and designed the detailed layout management adopted, fitting new equipment, benches and storage around machines that had to keep running. Phasing the prep and moves avoided an estimated $5,000 full-day shutdown.
role: I was responsible for the detailed layout and for coordinating between management and the floor; management made the major relocation decisions.
goal_constraints:
- Make room for new equipment without shutting the shop down.
- Keep required machine adjacencies and the service space around each machine.
- Improve access, safety, storage and findability (5S, with advice from a MassMEP consultant).
process_md:
- Interviewed machinists and watched daily work to learn what already worked and what got in the way.
- Built a to-scale SketchUp model and tagged every item: keep in place, move, remove, or review.
- Placed and oriented machines within management's major moves, drew each machine's service margin, and checked new hallway widths with 12, 8 and 5 ft gauge circles.
- Mapped which tasks had to finish before each stage could start, then sequenced prep and moves so machines kept running; helped take down workbenches, clear forklift paths and empty the back room.
- Relayed decisions to the floor and brought feedback back to management.
- Large-machine moves were underway when I left; floor resurfacing followed one to two weeks later.
lesson: Show before asking: I'd make a rough visual draft before taking an idea to my boss, so he could judge it faster.

media.caption: Final plan for the main floor, modeled to scale in SketchUp. Management set the major moves; I worked out machine orientation, exact placement, and where benches and storage fit. Colors: green = in final position, orange = planned, not yet moved, red = remove, purple = review, brown = work surface, yellow = keep contents. Large shaded margins = space needed to service a machine; white circles = 12, 8 and 5 ft gauges for checking the new hallway widths.
The original main-floor layout in the same view, with every item tagged keep in place, move, remove or review. Compare with the final plan at the top.

The dependency map I used to sequence the work: tasks (triangles) that had to finish before each stage (diamonds) could start, building toward the two goals in red: clearing space for the new machines and concrete pad, and redoing the detail room.
Eye level in the model, original layout: a crowded aisle of items marked for removal.
The same spot in the final plan: the aisle opens up.
Taking apart the built-in cabinet and counter in the hallway to open the route through the shop.
Before: the back room held the horizontal bandsaw, carts and racks of bar stock, and pallets; the compressor and tank sat on the back wall.
After: the same corner cleared for good; the compressor and tank stayed in place, wrapped while painters repainted the walls.
Before: plastic bar and sheet stock piled in a back-room corner beside the metal-stock rack.
After: the same corner with the plastics cleared and a flammables cabinet in their place, holding paints, solvents and oils.
Where the plastic stock went: a storage container outside the shop. I added the shelving and labeled it by material and size (UHMW, PVC, oversize) so it stays findable.
